paragraphs: Anesthesiologists (US counterpart O*NET/BLS 29-1211.00 Anesthesiologists) administer anesthetics and analgesics for pain management before, during, or after surgery: examine patients, take histories, and assess risks in surgical, obstetric, and other medical procedures using diagnostic tests; administer anesthesia or sedation during procedures via local, intravenous, spinal, or caudal routes; record anesthesia types, doses, and patient status throughout the procedure; monitor patients before, during, and after anesthesia and handle adverse reactions or complications; judge whether patients have recovered enough for transfer to another room, ward, or discharge home after outpatient surgery; coordinate anesthesia delivery with surgeons and patient positioning, and coordinate and direct the care by nurses, medical technicians, and other healthcare workers; maintain life support and airway management and prepare for emergency surgery; consult on anesthesia or sedation methods and approaches; manage anesthesia services and coordinate with other medical activities; place invasive vascular monitoring; order diagnostic tests such as laboratory and imaging; instruct and train students, residents, and staff; and conduct medical research and teaching. Practice requires first obtaining the physician qualification and registering, with anesthesia specialty qualifications and scope of practice constrained by law and institutional rules; this page is not medical, legal, or policy advice.

Paper tasks: using the complete fictional materials A/B/C in the entry exercise below, verify the plan document's version, review status, and authorization records, list discrepancies and items to confirm, and complete the three tasks and four works. The exercise contains no clinical data and involves no choice of anesthesia method, drugs, or abnormal thresholds; observe recording and collaboration habits — this cannot judge clinical ability or hiring.

Editorial self-check advice: observe whether you can verify materials item by item, keep unknowns, communicate clearly, and bear the applicable duties; also check the long-cycle medical training, on-call, protection, and continuous assessment conditions. The OOH also lists the anesthesiologists detail plus the larger physicians-and-surgeons combination of 862,800 persons, growth 4%, and 22,100 average annual openings, with a median wage of 275,930 USD — the combination does not replace this occupation.

In one sentence: a clinical specialty physician position that administers anesthesia and analgesia before, during, and after surgery, assesses and manages perioperative risks, leads airway and vital-sign management, and completes resuscitation handovers.

Anesthesiologists' work falls into four groups: preoperative evaluation and planning (examining patients, taking histories, assessing risks using diagnostic tests and laboratory work, consulting with other physicians to determine anesthesia or sedation methods and approaches, and ordering diagnostic tests); delivery and monitoring (administering anesthesia or sedation during procedures via local, intravenous, spinal, or caudal routes, coordinating anesthesia delivery with surgeons and positioning patients, placing invasive vascular monitoring, maintaining life support and airway management and preparing for emergency surgery, recording anesthesia types, doses, and patient status throughout, and monitoring patients and handling adverse reactions or complications); outcome judgment and team coordination (judging whether patients have recovered or stabilized enough for transfer to another room, ward, or discharge home after outpatient surgery, coordinating and directing nurses, medical technicians, and other healthcare workers, consulting and referring, and managing anesthesia services and coordinating with other medical activities); and teaching and research (instructing and training students, residents, and staff, teaching anesthesiology principles, conducting medical research to improve treatment and control disease, and arranging and maintaining operating-room and anesthesia sterilization equipment use).

O*NET 29-1211.00 Anesthesiologists: administer anesthetics and analgesics for pain management before, during, or after surgery. Common job titles include Anesthesiologist MD, Anesthesiology Resident, Attending Anesthesiologist, Cardiothoracic Anesthesiologist, Critical Care Anesthesiologist, Obstetric Anesthesiologist, Pediatric Anesthesiologist, and Physician (MD). O*NET wages and employment are specific to anesthesiologists; the interest code is ISR (Investigative, Social, Realistic).

The US O*NET 29-1211.00 respondent work context describes group answers, not Chinese positions or any individual's scheduling and risks:
Work hours｜99% have work weeks over 40 hours, and 94% have regular fixed schedules.
Exposure｜94% contact disease or infection daily; 52% contact contaminants daily, 13% at least once a week but not daily, and 15% never. Radiation exposure: 14% daily and 72% at least once a week but not daily. 68% wear common protective or safety equipment daily.
Precision and errors｜84% consider precision extremely important and 14% important; 83% consider the consequences of hard-to-correct errors extremely serious.
Communication｜98% are in continuous contact with others and 99% have face-to-face discussions daily; 65% consider dealing with external customers or the public extremely important.
Decisions and responsibility｜97% make decisions daily and 67% have a great deal of decision-making freedom; 92% consider their decisions very important to colleagues' or the organization's results, 74% bear very high responsibility for other workers' results, and 35% bear very high responsibility for others' health and safety.
Time pressure｜81% daily and 18% at least once a week but not daily.
Body posture｜97% work very close to others; 15% stand continuously or almost continuously and 69% sit less than half the time.
Conflict and collaboration｜17% encounter conflicts daily and 64% at least once a week but not daily; coordinating/leading others is considered extremely important by 35% and very important by 43%; group teamwork is considered very important by 14% and fairly important by 13%.

US MD/DO is a medical-school degree, not a license; the ASA describes anesthesiology residency training as four years, and practice additionally requires a state medical license. Sub-specialty fellowships are further training paths and must not be written as a universal threshold for everyone; BLS states that specialty board certification is not universally legally required. China's Physicians Law provides the qualification examination and registration, with application routes including a relevant medical bachelor's degree plus one year of supervised practice, or a practicing assistant physician plus two years of practice in the relevant specialty; the bachelor's route must not be written as the only path. The law establishes the standardized training framework, with specific position training, assessments, and authorizations checked against current competent-authority and institutional conditions. Medical documents, informed consent, and reporting obligations follow the Physicians Law and institutional rules. entries.answer: Examine patients, take medical histories, and evaluate perioperative risk with the help of diagnostic tests, consulting with other physicians to determine the type and method of anesthesia or sedation; during procedures administer anesthesia or sedation via local, intravenous, spinal, or caudal routes, place invasive intravascular monitoring, maintain life support and airway management, and prepare for emergency surgery; monitor patients before, during, and after anesthesia, record the anesthesia type, dosage, and patient status, and respond to adverse reactions or complications; judge whether a patient has recovered or stabilized enough to be transferred to another room or ward or to go home after outpatient surgery; coordinate and direct nurses, medical technicians, and other health care workers, and supervise residents and staff, conduct medical research, and manage anesthesia services.
entries.question: What does an anesthesiologist do every day?

entries.answer: Anesthesiologists evaluate, formulate, and implement anesthesia plans within lawful scope of practice and institutional authorization and are responsible for their own care and records; the ASA-described US anesthesia care team is led by anesthesiologists, who may delegate appropriate tasks while retaining overall responsibility. Assistants and nursing personnel still have their own professional obligations; CRNA authority varies by jurisdiction and institution. Monitoring, medication administration, recovery care, and follow-up may overlap among team members; these must not be excluded from physician tasks, nor may other team members be described as having no clinical judgment.

hero.quick_answer: Anesthesiologists administer anesthetics and analgesics for pain management before, during, or after surgery: they assess perioperative risk, consult with other physicians to determine the anesthesia or sedation method, administer anesthesia and place invasive monitoring, maintain life support and airway management, monitor patients throughout and respond to adverse reactions, judge the degree of recovery and complete the resuscitation handoff, while coordinating and directing the anesthesia team, conducting teaching and research, and managing anesthesia services. This page presents US OEWS anesthesiologist-specific wage percentiles and BLS employment projections (with the "Physicians and Surgeons" combination scope listed for contrast only); the China side provides only industry-scope and Physicians Law framework references; this page is not medical advice.

subject.name: Anesthesiologists
subject.summary: Anesthesiologists administer anesthetics and analgesics for pain management before, during, or after surgery: they assess perioperative risks, formulate and implement anesthesia plans, maintain airway and life support, monitor patients throughout and handle adverse reactions, judge recovery and complete resuscitation handovers, while coordinating and directing the anesthesia team, conducting teaching and research, and managing anesthesia services. Practice requires first obtaining the physician qualification and registering (the US side requires a licensed physician with completed anesthesia specialty training); scope of practice, specialty qualifications, and institutional authorization constrain clinical decisions.
